content: Many individuals with severe mental illness (SMI) have siblings who play a dual role: they can act as natural supporters in the recovery process of the affected individual, but they are also at risk of developing mental health issues themselves due to the negative impact of psychosis within the family. Despite substantial evidence showing that psychoeducation is effective in reducing relapse rates and improving treatment adherence for individuals with SMI and their families, siblings are often overlooked in both clinical settings and research studies. If psychoeducational interventions were specifically designed for siblings, they could enhance siblings' knowledge, coping mechanisms, and overall well-being, potentially offering a cost-effective way to support siblings while also improving outcomes for the individual with SMI. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of psychoeducation compared to usual care or other interventions in improving the well-being and reducing the distress of siblings of individuals with SMI. A secondary aim was to identify, if possible, which type of psychoeducation is most effective. To conduct this review, the Cochrane Schizophrenia Group Trials Register was searched, and reference lists of relevant reports and reviews were screened as of November 12, 2013. Trial authors were contacted to obtain unpublished data and specific information on outcomes for siblings. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that focused on psychoeducational interventions targeting siblings of individuals with SMI, delivered through various formats such as individual sessions, group settings, or computer-based programs. Two authors independently screened abstracts and extracted data, while two additional authors verified the process. Trial authors were contacted to clarify whether siblings participated in the studies and to obtain sibling-specific data when outcomes were grouped with those of other family members or caregivers. Risk differences (RD) and mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review identified 14 studies that included siblings among other family members receiving psychoeducational interventions. However, only one small trial provided relevant and available data specifically for siblings. This trial involved nine siblings out of 84 total participants and compared psychoeducation with standard care in a community care setting over 21 months. The evidence from this trial was insufficient to determine the effects of psychoeducation on siblings' quality of life (MD 3.80, 95% CI -0.26 to 7.86, low-quality evidence) or their ability to cope with family burden (MD -8.80, 95% CI -15.22 to -2.34, low-quality evidence). No siblings dropped out of the study within one year (RD 0.00, 95% CI -0.34 to 0.34, low-quality evidence). The evidence was also inadequate to assess the impact of psychoeducation on the clinical outcomes of individuals with SMI, including their global mental state (MD -0.60, 95% CI -3.54 to 2.38, low-quality evidence), frequency of re-hospitalization (MD -0.70, 95% CI -2.46 to 1.06, low-quality evidence), or duration of inpatient stay (MD -2.60, 95% CI -6.34 to 1.14, low-quality evidence), regardless of whether their siblings received psychoeducation. No data were available to evaluate other primary outcomes such as siblings' psychosocial well-being, distress, or adverse effects. In conclusion, most studies on psychoeducational interventions included siblings alongside other family members, but the proportion of siblings was small, and their outcomes were not reported separately. Only one study with nine siblings provided data for this review, and the evidence was of low quality and insufficient to determine whether psychoeducation benefits siblings' well-being or the clinical outcomes of individuals with SMI. More randomized studies are needed to explore the role of psychoeducation in addressing the specific needs of siblings for information and support.
